Let me start by reading the DESIGN.md file the user attached to understand the design reference. Then I need to research how to build this karaoke-like app with Spotify playback + listening to the user singing and singing the "other half" (i.e., playing the missing vocal parts).

Key challenges to research:
1. Spotify Web Playback SDK can play full songs in the browser (Premium required). But we cannot separate vocals from Spotify audio client-side easily? Actually, we can capture audio from the Spotify playback SDK via Web Audio API (the SDK gives an audio element; we can route it through Web Audio API using crossOrigin? Spotify iframes... Actually the Web Playback SDK plays through an <audio> element that can be accessed via `player.getCurrentState()`? The audio element itself is created inside the SDK. There are known tricks to grab the audio element and connect to Web Audio API. Some projects do this: spotify-web-playback-sdk audio element can be captured via document.querySelector('audio')? Hmm, it's inside an iframe? Let me recall: The Spotify Web Playback SDK creates a hidden audio element in the same document? I believe it's in the main document, and there's a known hack to grab it with document.querySelector('audio') and connect via createMediaElementSource. Several projects (e.g., "spotify-audio-visualizer") do this. Yes, it's possible.

2. Vocal separation: To sing "the other half" (the vocals the user is not singing), the app needs the original song's vocals separated from the backing track. Options:
   - Use a stem separation service/API (e.g., LALAL.AI API, Moises API, or run Demucs in the browser via ONNX? Too heavy). There are free/open APIs? Spleeter? Running server-side with Demucs.
   - Alternatively, play the instrumental/karaoke version and mute... wait, the user sings one part; the app should sing the OTHER half. So the app needs the full original track but with the parts the user sings removed — i.e., duck the original vocals when the user is singing (like "sing-along mode"), or actually perform vocal separation and play the vocal stem only during parts user doesn't sing.

   Simpler approach: The app plays the original song at lower volume (or with original vocals) and when the user sings, it... Hmm. The requirement: "listens to me singing and sings the other half of the song which I am not singing for me". This is like a duet with the app. The app needs to know the song's vocal melody/timing. Without lyrics alignment data, hard.

   Practical execution: Use Spotify audio + real-time vocal separation is not feasible client-side quickly. Alternative: Use the original track, and when user sings (detected via mic pitch/energy), duck the track's vocal portion — but we can't separate vocals in real time in browser with low latency... Actually there are lightweight real-time vocal removal approaches (center-channel cancellation) which remove mid-panned vocals — that's a classic karaoke trick. Spotify streams are decoded locally, so we can apply stereo mid/side processing in real time to create "instrumental-ish" and "vocal-ish" stems. Center extraction gives vocals; side gives instruments. This is real-time and feasible via Web Audio API with ChannelSplitter + gain inversion.

   So architecture:
   - Play song via Spotify Web Playback SDK (Premium account required — user has Spotify developer account; need Premium for playback; note that).
   - Capture the audio element into Web Audio graph.
   - Build a "vocal reducer" (center channel cancellation) to get instrumental; also center-channel extraction to get vocals.
   - When user sings (voice activity detection via mic analysis), crossfade: user sings → play instrumental (center cancelled); user stops → play original (full mix) so the app "sings" the parts user isn't singing. Wait, but that would replay the vocals the user just sang too. The user wants the app to sing the other half — i.e., during the user's singing parts, app is silent (user sings over instrumental), and during non-singing parts, the app sings (original vocals play). That's essentially "intelligent karaoke ducking": the original track plays, but during user singing we duck/remove the original vocals so user can take over. This matches "sings the other half of the song which I am not singing".

   That's buildable! The mic listens for voice activity, and we crossfade between full mix and center-cancelled mix. Latency is fine.

   Even better: use Moises API or LALAL.AI to get real stems (server-side, per track, requires paid API). We can offer that as an optional enhancement, but core works with the center-channel trick without any external separation service. Since user wants "no placeholder data, ready to use", the app should work with real Spotify credentials.

   Also Spotify provides audio analysis? The Web API audio-features/audio-analysis endpoints were deprecated for new apps in Nov 2024 (audio features, recommendations etc. restricted). So don't rely on audio-analysis for section detection. Could use playback position to compute lyrics timing? No lyrics API. Could optionally use lyrics from lrclib.net (free, no key) to get synced lyrics! That could enable "sections" detection: show lyrics, highlight, and detect user singing. lrclib provides synced LRC lyrics for many songs — free public API. That would enhance the karaoke feel: display synced lyrics. That's a nice addition without keys. But careful: don't overpromise. We can integrate lrclib as best-effort.

   Hmm, but "sings the other half" — the app can't actually generate vocals (TTS singing) without a singing-synthesis service. Realistic interpretation: the original artist's vocals from the track serve as the "other half". The ducking approach achieves the duet feel. I should explain this clearly in research summary.

3. Tech stack: Single-page web app. Vanilla JS/TS + Vite? Or Next.js? The DESIGN.md will inform. Let me read it first.

Plan:

- Research: Spotify Web Playback SDK requirements (Premium), capturing audio element, browser autoplay policies, mic permissions, Web Audio ducking. Also check current state 2026: Spotify deprecated some endpoints; check Web Playback SDK docs; check lrclib availability.
- Build the app in D:\EPIC\Dev_Web\closer.
- Design per DESIGN.md, no AI-generated icons/images; use CSS? User says "don't use any artificial icons, images made with css, use placeholder instead" — meaning: for icons/images, use placeholders (e.g., generic placeholder images like via placeholder services? or simple neutral blocks). Hmm "images made with css" — they don't want CSS-drawn fake icons; use placeholders instead. So album art: Spotify API provides real album art — that's real data, fine. Icons: avoid icon libraries; use placeholders? That seems odd for production readiness. I'll interpret: no fabricated icon art; where an icon/image is needed but no real asset, use a simple placeholder (e.g., a neutral rounded rectangle with a letter/label, or picsum/placeholder image). Real Spotify album art and real data everywhere.

- No placeholder data: app must fetch real data from Spotify API (user's playlists, tracks). Auth via PKCE OAuth (client-side, no server needed). Client ID from user's developer account — they said they can provide API key. I should build with a config where user enters Client ID (stored in localStorage) or .env. Since no backend, PKCE is the way. The redirect URI must be whitelisted in their Spotify dashboard — I'll document.

1: # LoreSign Design System
2: 
3: The homepage is the visual source of truth for LoreSign. New marketing pages,
4: product surfaces and lifecycle emails should feel like they belong to the same
5: brand, even when their density and interaction patterns differ.
6: 
7: Canonical implementation:
8: 
9: - `frontend/src/app/page.tsx`
10: - `frontend/src/components/home/*`
11: - `frontend/src/components/home/landing.css`
12: - `frontend/src/components/app/SiteNav.tsx`
13: - `frontend/src/components/ui/button-styles.css`
14: - `frontend/src/app/globals.css`
15: 
16: This document describes the design currently rendered by those files. If the
17: homepage and this document disagree, verify the rendered homepage first, then
18: update this document with the intentional change.
19: 
20: ## 1. Design character
21: 
22: LoreSign is calm, direct and modern. It should make legal-document work feel
23: clear rather than ceremonial.
24: 
25: The visual language combines:
26: 
27: - editorial typography and generous white space;
28: - near-black text and dark storytelling sections;
29: - one vivid blue family for actions, emphasis and product imagery;
30: - product screenshots and purpose-built illustrations instead of generic
31:   stock photography;
32: - thin grey rules for structure;
33: - soft elevation only where it adds hierarchy;
34: - restrained motion that makes the interface feel responsive and crafted.
35: 
36: The result should feel trustworthy and approachable, not corporate-heavy,
37: playful, glassy or ornamental.
38: 
39: ## 2. Brand and copy
40: 
41: - The product name is **LoreSign**, with a capital L and S, in all visible copy.
42: - Use sentence case for headings, buttons, navigation and labels.
43: - Prefer short, concrete phrases: “Create your document”, “Send and track”,
44:   “Questions, answered.”
45: - Explain benefits in plain language. Avoid legal jargon unless accuracy
46:   requires it.
47: - CTA labels name the next action: “Get Started”, “Choose Pro”, “Watch Demo”.
48: - Ampersands are acceptable in compact display headlines, as used in the hero.
49: 
50: ## 3. Typography
51: 
52: LoreSign uses a two-font system.
53: 
54: | Role | Typeface | Weights | Notes |
55: |---|---|---:|---|
56: | Display and headings | Sora | 600, 700 | Geometric, compact and confident |
57: | Body, navigation and controls | Urbanist | 400, 500, 600, 700 | Open and readable |
58: 
59: Implementation variables are `--font-sora` and `--font-urbanist`. The global
60: Tailwind `font-sans` token resolves to Urbanist. Marketing headings inside
61: `.landing-section` and `.landing-footer` use Sora.
62: 
63: ### Marketing type scale
64: 
65: | Element | Desktop | Mobile | Typical treatment |
66: |---|---:|---:|---|
67: | Hero h1 | 56px | `clamp(28px, 7vw, 42px)` | 600, 1.26 line-height, tight tracking |
68: | Section h2 | 48px | 32px | 600, 1.15-1.25 line-height |
69: | Closing CTA h2 | 44px | 32px | 700, 1.3 line-height on mobile |
70: | Card/step h3 | 20-24px | 17-24px | 600 |
71: | Hero introduction | 18px | 16px | 24px line-height |
72: | Body | 16px | 16px | 22-26px line-height |
73: | Supporting metadata | 14px | 14px | Use sparingly |
74: 
75: Keep display headings compact and intentional. Body copy should usually stay
76: between 55 and 75 characters per line. Do not use condensed all-caps labels as
77: a default visual device.
78: 
79: ## 4. Colour
80: 
81: Use the semantic tokens in `globals.css` for UI work. The homepage also uses a
82: small number of branded marketing colours in its patterned artwork and CTA
83: gradient.
84: 
85: ### Core palette
86: 
87: | Token / role | Value | Usage |
88: |---|---|---|
89: | `--bg`, `--bg-card` | `#ffffff` | Main canvas, cards and light sections |
90: | `--surface-2`, `--bg-elev` | `#f7f7f7` | Quiet fills, disabled states and hover surfaces |
91: | `--fg` | `#1a1a1a` | Primary text and dark section background |
92: | `--fg-muted` | `#4b5563` | Body copy on light backgrounds |
93: | `--fg-subtle` | `#666666` | Navigation and secondary labels |
94: | `--fg-faint` | `#717171` | Captions and helper text |
95: | `--accent` | `#1457ff` | Primary blue, links, focus and emphasis |
96: | `--accent-hover` | `#0b46d8` | Simple blue hover state |
97: | `--accent-tint` | `#f5f7ff` | Selected and lightly emphasized surfaces |
98: | `--border` | `#e6e6e6` | Hairlines and section dividers |
99: | `--border-strong` | `#d9d9d9` | Stronger neutral boundaries |
100: | `--border-control` | `#949494` | Accessible control outlines |
101: | Hero pattern base | `#a8d4ff` | Blue patterned media stages |
102: | Primary CTA highlight | `#6a95ff` | Top of the primary CTA gradient |
103: 
104: Dark sections use `#1a1a1a` with white headings. Supporting copy is softened
105: to roughly 80% white or a light grey such as `#e5e7eb`. Footer copy uses a
106: quieter grey, currently `#9ca3af`.
107: 
108: Use blue deliberately. It identifies an action, selection, link or branded
109: visual moment. Most of the page should remain white, near-black and neutral.
110: Do not introduce additional competing brand colours.
111: 
112: ## 5. Shape, borders and elevation
113: 
114: The system has one primary corner radius: **8px**. All radius tokens currently
115: resolve to 8px.
116: 
117: Use 8px for:
118: 
119: - buttons and controls;
120: - marketing cards;
121: - image and video frames;
122: - dialogs and dropdowns;
123: - feature panels and pricing cards.
124: 
125: Use circles only for inherently circular elements such as avatars, status
126: dots and play controls.
127: 
128: Borders are usually 1px `--border`. They separate content without making every
129: element feel boxed. Use shared seams and dividers for comparison layouts and
130: content grids.
131: 
132: Shadows are selective, not forbidden:
133: 
134: - primary CTAs have a soft blue shadow and subtle inset highlight;
135: - secondary marketing actions may have a very light neutral shadow;
136: - product previews and feature cards may use low-opacity elevation;
137: - ordinary product cards and dense application rows should rely on borders.
138: 
139: Avoid heavy drop shadows, multiple floating layers, glass effects and blur
140: glows.
141: 
142: ## 6. Layout and spacing
143: 
144: ### Widths
145: 
146: - Standard marketing content: `max-width: 1120px`.
147: - Navigation and pricing: up to `1300px`.
148: - Footer inner content: up to `1440px`.
149: - Long-form copy remains much narrower inside those containers.
150: 
151: ### Section rhythm
152: 
153: - Standard desktop marketing section: 60px vertical, 24px horizontal.
154: - Standard mobile marketing section: 48px vertical, 20px horizontal.
155: - Dark workflow section: 80px vertical.
156: - Closing CTA: 80px top and 60px bottom on desktop.
157: - Section heading stack: 12px between title and copy, about 40px before the
158:   section content; reduce the content gap to about 28px on mobile.
159: - Use 20, 24, 32, 40, 48, 60 and 80px as the main spacing rhythm.
160: 
161: Layouts should feel open, but spacing must still communicate grouping. Keep
162: related copy close and use the larger steps between distinct ideas.
163: 
164: ## 7. Signature homepage patterns
165: 
166: ### Navigation
167: 
168: - Fixed white bar with a thin bottom border.
169: - Small LoreSign mark on the left, primary links centred on desktop and account
170:   actions on the right.
171: - Navigation labels are 14px Urbanist medium.
172: - Mobile uses a 75px bar and a simple three-line menu trigger.
173: - Dropdowns are white, 8px, bordered and lightly elevated.
174: 
175: ### Hero
176: 
177: - Centred, high-contrast headline and concise supporting paragraph.
178: - Primary and secondary CTAs sit together as a compact action group.
179: - The main product preview sits inside a large blue patterned stage.
180: - The product screenshot is the proof. Keep it large enough to read as a real
181:   interface, not a decorative thumbnail.
182: 
183: ### Proof and benefit grids
184: 
185: - Pair simple custom illustrations with short benefit statements.
186: - Use column dividers instead of separate floating cards when the content forms
187:   one comparison or story.
188: - Icons and artwork are much larger than ordinary interface icons.
189: 
190: ### Dark workflow
191: 
192: - Use a near-black full-width band to change pace and focus attention.
193: - White headings and softened white body copy keep contrast clear.
194: - Present steps as a vertical narrative with large product visuals.
195: - The dark band is a major storytelling device, not a default card colour.
196: 
197: ### Feature gallery
198: 
199: - Feature cards use a roughly 42/58 copy-to-visual split on desktop.
200: - Copy includes one focused title, a short explanation and two proof points.
201: - Product artwork fills the visual pane and uses the blue pattern where useful.
202: - The homepage pins and transitions between feature cards while scrolling.
203:   Without motion, the cards must still form a complete readable sequence.
204: 
205: ### Recipient experience
206: 
207: - A central video/product moment is framed by four concise benefit cells.
208: - Shared borders connect the cells into one system.
209: - At intermediate widths, benefit cells become pairs around a full-width video;
210:   on small screens they stack.
211: 
212: ### Pricing
213: 
214: - Four plans form a comparison grid on large screens and a gapped grid below.
215: - The recommended plan is identified with an accent border, pale tint and
216:   “Most popular” label.
217: - Prices have strong typographic contrast; feature rows stay aligned and use
218:   consistent check/cross icons.
219: - Only the recommended plan receives the primary gradient action. Other plan
220:   actions are white with a quiet border and blue label.
221: 
222: ### FAQ
223: 
224: - Two columns on desktop: introduction on the left, accordion on the right.
225: - Accordion rows use horizontal rules rather than individual cards.
226: - Questions are 18px semibold; answers are 16px with generous leading.
227: - Plus/minus imagery communicates the state without adding visual noise.
228: 
229: ### Closing CTA and footer
230: 
231: - The closing CTA returns to the near-black background and a two-column layout.
232: - The footer continues the same dark surface, separated by a subtle rule.
233: - Footer navigation is compact and muted, with white group headings.
234: - The oversized dotted LoreSign wordmark is a branded finish, not ordinary
235:   page content.
236: 
237: ## 8. Buttons and actions
238: 
239: ### Primary marketing CTA
240: 
241: - 54px minimum height, 8px radius, 16px semibold Urbanist.
242: - Vertical gradient from `#6a95ff` to `#1457ff`.
243: - Soft blue drop shadow plus a faint inner bottom highlight.
244: - The illustrated “Get Started” treatment includes the white signature/arrow
245:   tile on the right.
246: 
247: ### Secondary marketing action
248: 
249: - White surface, subtle border and light neutral shadow.
250: - Near-black label with a blue circular play icon when used for demos.
251: - In dark sections, use the dark secondary treatment rather than a white card.
252: 
253: ### Interaction
254: 
255: - Marketing CTAs use the shared `.marketing-flip` treatment: a near-black
256:   reveal and a vertical label roll over about 350ms.
257: - Keyboard focus uses a visible 3px blue outline with offset.
258: - Disabled actions use the quiet neutral surface and readable muted text, not
259:   reduced opacity.
260: - Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`; preserve the state change without the roll.
261: 
262: Application actions may be denser, but they should reuse the same colour,
263: radius, type and focus language through the primitives in
264: `frontend/src/components/ui`.
265: 
266: ## 9. Imagery and iconography
267: 
268: - Prefer real product screens, annotated product states and custom vector or
269:   raster illustrations.
270: - Blue halftone/wave patterns are a brand asset. Use them as contained stages,
271:   never as a full-page background behind body copy.
272: - Screenshots should be crisp, aligned and clipped cleanly at 8px corners.
273: - Marketing illustrations may use internal shadows and colours that are part of
274:   the artwork; surrounding UI should continue to use semantic tokens.
275: - Interface icons should remain simple outline forms with consistent stroke
276:   weight. Do not mix unrelated icon styles in one surface.
277: - Large circular play controls are reserved for video.
278: 
279: ## 10. Motion
280: 
281: Motion should reinforce hierarchy and continuity.
282: 
283: Current homepage behaviours include:
284: 
285: - Lenis-assisted smooth scrolling;
286: - a GSAP/ScrollTrigger pinned feature sequence;
287: - 300ms accordion and menu transitions;
288: - 350ms CTA reveal and label roll;
289: - a subtle pulsing video-play affordance;
290: - small opacity, position and scale changes between feature states.
291: 
292: Every animated experience needs a complete static fallback. Disable nonessential
293: transitions and scroll choreography under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`.
294: Do not animate basic reading content merely to make the page feel busy.
295: 
296: ## 11. Responsive behaviour
297: 
298: Design mobile layouts deliberately rather than shrinking desktop.
299: 
300: - The primary layout breakpoint is 768px; desktop-specific composition becomes
301:   prominent at 1024px.
302: - Section padding moves from 24px to 20px at mobile widths.
303: - Headings scale down while retaining strong contrast and short line lengths.
304: - Action groups wrap with a 12px gap and must remain fully usable at 320px.
305: - Multi-column proof, feature, recipient, pricing, FAQ and footer layouts stack
306:   or become two-column grids according to available space.
307: - Product previews retain their aspect ratio and crop intentionally.
308: - The feature gallery measures its mobile copy and artwork so pinned states do
309:   not overlap.
310: - The footer becomes two columns, with the brand statement spanning both.
311: 
312: Check at minimum: 390px mobile, 768px tablet, 1024px small desktop and 1440px
313: desktop.
314: 
315: ## 12. Application surfaces
316: 
317: The application is denser than the homepage, but it is not a separate visual
318: brand.
319: 
320: - Keep Urbanist as the default interface font and Sora for meaningful page or
321:   section headings.
322: - Reuse the same white canvas, near-black text, LoreSign blue, 8px radius and
323:   grey border system.
324: - Prefer borders and grouping over decorative shadow in dashboards, editors,
325:   tables and settings.
326: - Use the primitives in `frontend/src/components/ui` for buttons, fields,
327:   dialogs, sheets, menus, tabs, banners, badges, progress, loading and empty
328:   states.
329: - Keep the marketing gradient and flip animation for prominent acquisition or
330:   upgrade moments. Routine product actions should remain calmer.
331: - Status colours are semantic and must not compete with the brand blue.
332: 
333: ## 13. Accessibility and quality bar
334: 
335: - Body and control text must meet WCAG AA contrast.
336: - All interactive controls need a visible keyboard focus state.
337: - Keep touch targets at least 44 by 44px, or provide an equivalent expanded hit
338:   area.
339: - Never encode state by colour alone. Pair it with copy, an icon, border or
340:   position.
341: - Decorative images use empty alt text. Product screenshots and meaningful
342:   media need concise descriptions.
343: - Accordions, dialogs, menus and tabs must expose their state to assistive
344:   technology.
345: - Motion must respect reduced-motion preferences.
346: - Verify marketing work visually at desktop and mobile, not only through type
347:   checking.
348: 
349: ## 14. Do and do not
350: 
351: Do:
352: 
353: - lead with one clear message and one obvious next action;
354: - alternate calm white sections with a small number of high-impact brand
355:   moments;
356: - use Sora for display hierarchy and Urbanist for reading and controls;
357: - let product screens and purpose-built artwork carry the proof;
358: - reuse the shared navigation, action, card and footer patterns;
359: - keep edges, typography and spacing consistent.
360: 
361: Do not:
362: 
363: - replace the homepage aesthetic with generic SaaS gradients or glass cards;
364: - cover every card with a shadow;
365: - introduce a rainbow of accent colours;
366: - use pill-shaped cards or controls by default;
367: - apply the patterned blue background behind long-form copy;
368: - add motion without a reduced-motion and static state;
369: - invent one-off typography, radius or button treatments when a shared pattern
370:   already exists.
371:

Known fact: Many people have connected Spotify playback to visualizers. There's a documented approach: the SDK renders an <audio> element with src set to a blob: or https URL. Some repos: "spotify-web-visualizer" uses Web Audio on the SDK audio element successfully. I recall reading that the audio element src is cross-origin (audio-ssl.spotifycdn.com) and those URLs DO include CORS headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *), allowing crossOrigin="anonymous" to be set. Hmm, not 100% sure.

Let me research with websearch to confirm feasibility. This is the "make sure this can be built" part. I should verify:
1. Web Playback SDK + Web Audio API capture feasibility.
2. If that fails, fallback: user uploads the song file (no), or use another music source (YouTube? TOS issues). Spotify is required by user.
3. Center channel extraction quality on Spotify streams (stereo, mostly mid-panned vocals → works decently; modern mixes have wide vocals though).

Actually wait — there's a cleaner modern option: real stem separation. In 2025/2026, there are browser-capable separation models? Running Demucs via transformers.js? Demucs v4 ONNX in browser is heavy (~80MB+ per model, WASM slow). There are services: Moises API (paid), LALAL.AI API (paid), AudioShake (paid). For a local dev app, we could pre-process: user picks song → we call a separation API → get instrumental/vocal stems URL → play stems synced with Spotify? That's complex and costs money.

Better plan for v1 (buildable, zero external deps, works today):
- Spotify playback via Web Playback SDK.
- Real-time center-channel processing to derive two mixes: "Full mix" (original) and "No-vocals" (center-cancelled instrumental).
- Mic monitoring: when user's voice detected (energy + spectral features), fade from full mix toward instrumental (duck the original vocals so the user takes the lead); when the user stops, bring original vocals back = the app "sings".
- Actually invert: default state = full mix (app singing). When user sings = instrumental state (user sings). This literally means "the app sings the half you're not singing".
- Synced lyrics via lrclib (free, no key) to display the words, and optional "you're on" highlighting based on detected vocal activity... Actually better: use lyric timestamps? We don't know which lines the user will sing — it's free-form duet. The ducking handles it organically.

Enhancement (optional, if user wants later): a real stem-separation service.

I should also verify Spotify Web API scopes needed: streaming, user-read-email, user-read-private, user-modify-playback-state, playlist-read-private. PKCE flow with local redirect (http://127.0.0.1:PORT/callback or the dev URL). Spotify now requires https or loopback IP for redirect URIs (http://127.0.0.1 allowed, localhost discouraged but allowed?). In April 2025 Spotify announced requirements: redirect URIs must use HTTPS except loopback (127.0.0.1) for development. Also they enforce explicit redirect URI matching. For local dev with Vite, use http://127.0.0.1:5173/callback.

Also note: Web Playback SDK requires Premium. The user has a Spotify developer account but their personal account must be Premium for in-browser playback. If they don't have Premium, playback won't work — need to flag. Alternative if no Premium: cannot stream via Spotify SDK (30s previews only, and those are mp3 URLs we can play through audio element with CORS? previews are mp3 128kbps and CORS-enabled historically. But full songs needed → Premium.)

Also the November 2024 API changes: for apps in development mode, restricted endpoints (audio-features, recommendations, etc.) return 403. Playlist read, search, profile, player control still fine.

Now the lyrics: lrclib.net — free public API, no auth: https://lrclib.net/api/search?track_name=...&artist_name=... returns syncedLyrics (LRC). Rate limit friendly usage. This gives karaoke-style synced lyrics display. It's "ready to use with no placeholder data" — real lyrics fetched live. If no lyrics found, show "no synced lyrics available" gracefully.

Mic → Web Audio: getUserMedia, AnalyserNode, compute RMS energy + spectral centroid/band energy to detect singing vs. background. Simple adaptive threshold + hysteresis + hold time. Also show user's pitch? Could add a pitch display (autocorrelation) for fun — maybe show detected note for feedback ("sing detection" indicator). Keep scope sane: VAD with energy + high-frequency-band ratio, plus optional simple pitch track via autocorrelation to display note. That's doable in vanilla JS.

Echo/feedback consideration: user sings while speakers play — that's normal karaoke; the mic detects the user's voice but also hears the speakers (the full mix playing). If we duck based on detecting "voice" while speakers play vocals, feedback loop: app's vocals playing through speakers would trigger the mic VAD → never ducks. Mitigation: spectral comparison? Simple approach: VAD threshold on mic energy relative to... The mic will pick up the music too. Options:
- Recommend headphones (standard for karaoke apps). Document clearly: "use headphones for best duet detection". With headphones, mic only hears user's voice → clean detection.
- Without headphones, mic hears everything → detection unreliable. We can add "mic sensitivity" slider and a "push to sing" manual mode fallback: hold Space / press button to take the lead. That's a solid, honest fallback: auto mode (headphones) + manual mode.

Also add a "vocal sensitivity" calibration step before starting: "stay quiet for 2 seconds" to set noise floor.

Architecture decision: vanilla HTML/CSS/JS with Vite? Or Next.js? Design doc references Next.js/React patterns (globals.css, components). But for a solo local app, a Vite vanilla TS project is leaner. The design doc's "canonical implementation" is for LoreSign, not closer — we just borrow the visual language. I'll go with Vite + TypeScript (no framework) — fewer moving parts, easy for user to run: npm install, npm run dev. Hmm, but state management (auth, player, UI) in vanilla TS is fine with a small store.

Actually, let me reconsider: React would help with the duet UI (lyrics list, progress, states). But vanilla TS with careful DOM code is fine and lighter. I'll use Vite vanilla-ts. Also need to serve over http://127.0.0.1 for Spotify redirect.

Fonts: Sora + Urbanist from Google Fonts (real CDN). Icons: user said no artificial icons, no CSS-drawn images, use placeholders instead. So for icons use... placeholders? I think they mean: don't fabricate icon artwork; where an image/icon is needed use a placeholder. I'll minimize icons entirely — text labels + a few inline SVG outline icons? Inline SVGs are "artificial icons"? They said don't use artificial icons or CSS images, use placeholders. Safest: no icon fonts/libraries, no CSS-drawn art. Use text-only buttons and, where a visual is genuinely needed (e.g., album art before it loads), a neutral placeholder (grey block with label "Artwork"). Real album art comes from Spotify CDN = real data, allowed. For play/pause, use text labels "Play"/"Pause" — simple and honest. Actually small inline SVG glyphs like a triangle for play... that's an icon. User explicitly said no. Use text. OK.

Let me now research to verify the critical Spotify technical facts. Searches:
1. "Spotify Web Playback SDK Web Audio API audio element capture visualizer"
2. "Spotify Web Playback SDK audio element iframe createMediaElementSource"
3. "Spotify API deprecated endpoints November 2024 audio features recommendations"
4. "Spotify redirect URI http 127.0.0.1 requirements 2025"
5. "lrclib API synced lyrics"
6. Maybe "center channel extraction karaoke web audio" (I know this well enough).

Let me run several websearches in parallel.

The design doc gives me a clear visual language to adapt (Sora/Urbanist, white canvas, near-black text, `#1457ff` blue, 8px radii, thin borders — adapted for "closer"). The working directory is empty, so we're building from scratch. Introducing some changes to our Web API | Spotify for Developers

Introducing some changes to our Web API

Posted November 27, 2024

Spotify

Since our last broader update on the Community platform, we continue to see new integrations made through Spotify’s APIs and SDKs. We’re excited about the continued engagement we’re seeing to learn, experiment, innovate, and deliver unique experiences with Spotify.

As we continue to review the experience provided on Spotify for Developers, we've decided to roll out a number of measures with the aim of creating a more secure platform.

## Web API endpoint integration

Effective today, new Web API use cases will no longer be able to access or use the following endpoints and functionality in their third-party applications. Applications with existing extended mode Web API access that were relying on these endpoints remain unaffected by this change.

These changes will impact the following Web API applications:

## [Web API Reference | Spotify for Developers](https://developer.spotify.com/documentation/web-api/reference/get-recommendations)

# Get Recommendations 

Deprecated

Recommendations are generated based on the available information for a given seed entity and matched against similar artists and tracks. If there is sufficient information about the provided seeds, a list of tracks will be returned together with pool size details.

For artists and tracks that are very new or obscure there might not be enough data to generate a list of tracks.

 Important policy note

- Spotify content may not be used to train machine learning or AI model

Please note that you can not use the Spotify Platform or any Spotify Content to train a machine learning or AI model or otherwise ingesting Spotify Content into a machine learning or AI model.

More information

Part of the response when Track Relinking is applied. If `true`, the track is playable in the given market. Otherwise `false`.

Deprecated

Part of the response when Track Relinking is applied, and the requested track has been replaced with different track. The track in the `linked_from` object contains information about the originally requested track.
- restrictions object 

Included in the response when a content restriction is applied.

- reason string 

The reason for the restriction. Supported values:

- `market` - The content item is not available in the given market.
- `product` - The content item is not available for the user's subscription type.
- `explicit` - The content item is explicit and the user's account is set to not play explicit content.

Additional reasons may be added in the future. Note: If you use this field, make sure that your application safely handles unknown values.
- name string 

The name of the track.
- popularity integer 

Deprecated

The popularity of the track. The value will be between 0 and 100, with 100 being the most popular. The popularity of a track is a value between 0 and 100, with 100 being the most popular. The popularity is calculated by algorithm and is based, in the most part, on the total number of plays the track has had and how recent those plays are. Generally speaking, songs that are being played a lot now will have a higher popularity than songs that were played a lot in the past. Duplicate tracks (e.g. the same track from a single and an album) are rated independently. Artist and album popularity is derived mathematically from track popularity. Note: the popularity value may lag actual popularity by a few days: the value is not updated in real time.

## [Spotify Audio Features Is Dead: What to Use in 2026](https://freqblog.com/blog/spotify-audio-features-replacement-2026/)
Published: 2026-05-08T01:12:01.000Z

On November 27, 2024, Spotify deprecated `audio_features`, `audio_analysis`, recommendations, related artists, and featured playlists in one quiet developer-blog post. New apps got 403s the same day. Nearly two years later, there is still no official replacement — and the February 2026 changes made the rest of the Web API harder to use, not easier.

If you built anything that depended on BPM, key, danceability, energy, valence, or any of the other 11 numbers Spotify used to hand out for free, you've already had to replace it or you're maintaining a fork that exists only because of one grandfathered token.

...

## What actually died, in one table

| Endpoint | What it gave you | Status (May 2026) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/audio-features/{id}` | BPM, key, mode, danceability, energy, valence, acousticness, instrumentalness, liveness, loudness, speechiness, time_signature | 403 for new apps |
| `/audio-analysis/{id}` | Per-bar / per-beat / per-segment analysis with timestamps and pitches | 403 for new apps |
| `/recommendations` | Genre-seed and feature-seed recommendations | 403 for new apps |
| `/artists/{id}/related-artists` | Up to 20 related artists | 403 for new apps |
| `/browse/featured-playlists` | Editorial curation lists | 403 for new apps |
| `/browse/categories/{id}/playlists` | Playlists in a genre category | 403 for new apps |
| `/me/top/{tracks|artists}` | User listening history | Still live, but Web API Dev Mode (Feb 2026) cut the cap from 25 users to 5 without quota extension |

Apps that had a quota extension in flight on November 27, 2024 are still live. Everyone else gets 403. There is no path to access these endpoints for a new app, no waitlist, and no public statement that this will change.

...

The honest read is that Spotify never wanted to host this data in the first place. The `audio_features` endpoint is a thin wrapper around analysis Spotify acquired when they bought The Echo Nest in 2014,. Returning eleven floats for every track in a 100-million-track catalog costs Spotify infrastructure for zero strategic value — nobody's paying premium for "give me the BPM of Blinding Lights."

Worse for developers: the `recommendations` endpoint was a competitive liability. Letting any third party build a Spotify-quality recommender by spamming `seed_genres=house&target_energy=0.8` queries undermined the whole "premium algorithm" pitch. Killing it makes commercial sense for Spotify even though it leaves thousands of apps broken.

...

The right one is "what's the smallest dependency I can rebuild this on so I'm never one PR-merge away from being broken again?"

...

### Pattern 2: Feature-range filtering

If you were doing the `recommendations`-with-target-features dance:

```
# Spotify (deprecated)
GET /v1/recommendations?seed_genres=house&target_energy=0.8&min_tempo=120

# FreqBlog — direct drop-ins for the two killed endpoints
GET /recommendations?seed_tracks=<id>&limit=20   # replaces /v1/recommendations
GET /related-artists?artist=<name>&limit=20      # replaces /artists/{id}/related-artists
# …or filter the catalog by genre or tempo, or rank by similarity
GET /genres/house/tracks?limit=20
GET /bpm?bpm=120&tolerance=4&limit=20

```

Different endpoints, same goal. FreqBlog exposes a similarity-based recommender (`/similar?track_id=...`) that doesn't require seed-genre tuning — pass a track you like, get back the 10 acoustically nearest neighbours, ranked on a PANNs audio embedding of how each track sounds blended with cosine similarity over an 18-feature embedding.

...

### Is the Spotify Audio Features API still available?

No. Spotify deprecated the `/audio-features` and `/audio-analysis` endpoints on 27 November 2024. Apps that didn't already have extended access now receive `403` errors, and there's no official replacement.

...

### Why did Spotify remove the audio features endpoint?

Spotify restricted `audio-features`, `audio-analysis`, `recommendations` and several other endpoints to existing apps as part of a broad Web API lockdown announced on 27 November 2024. It hasn't signalled any plan to restore them.

Key findings so far:
1. Spotify deprecated audio-features/audio-analysis/recommendations for new apps (Nov 2024). Also Feb 2026 changes reduced dev mode cap from 25 users to 5. So I must NOT rely on audio-analysis for section detection. Core endpoints (playlists, tracks, search, profile, player control) still work.
2. Web Playback SDK + Web Audio: The kaleidosync project is mentioned — but kaleidosync uses the SDK... Actually kaleidosync uses Web Audio with the SDK? I recall kaleidosync had issues and used... Hmm, the comment says "I believe it is now possible to get analyzer data because I saw this recently: kaleidosync" — kaleidosync actually used the deprecated audio-analysis API, not real-time capture. ## [Redirect URIs | Spotify for Developers](https://developer.spotify.com/documentation/web-api/concepts/redirect%5Furi)

# Redirect URIs 

Beginning on the 9th of April 2025 we will enforce the subsequent validations to all newly created apps.

We expect all clients to migrate to the new redirect URI validation by November 2025.

To know more please refer to the Spotify Developer Blog.

When you create an app, you need to specify a redirect URI. This is the URI to which Spotify redirects the user after they have granted or denied permission to your app. The redirect URI is required for the authorization code flow and implicit grant flow. The definition of the redirect URI must exactly match the redirect URI you provide when you create your app. The only exception is for loopback IP literals, which can dynamically be assigned ports.

## Requirements

Since we at Spotify, take security very seriously you must follow these requirements when defining your redirect URI:

- Use HTTPS for your redirect URI, unless you are using a loopback address, when HTTP is permitted.
- If you are using a loopback address, use the explicit IPv4 or IPv6, like `http://127.0.0.1:PORT` or `http://[::1]:PORT` as your redirect URI.
- `localhost` is not allowed as redirect URI.

### Loopback addresses and port numbers

When using a loopback IP literal, you might not know the port number used in advance if it can be assigned dynamically. If you don't know the port number in advance, register your redirect URI with a loopback IP literal, but without any port number. You can add the dynamically assigned port number to the redirect URI in the authorization request. Please note that this is only supported for loopback IP literals, and not for other redirect URIs. This is on-par with the IETF recommendations.

## Examples

Here are some examples of redirect URIs:

1

 https://example.com/callback 

 http://127.0.0.1:8000/callback

## [Migrate away from Insecure Redirect URIs | Spotify for Developers](https://developer.spotify.com/documentation/web-api/tutorials/migration-insecure-redirect-uri)

Spotify is deprecating the use of insecure redirect URIs. This guide will help you migrate your application to use secure redirect URIs. To better understand which redirect URIs are considered secure, please refer to the Redirect URI guide.

...

## Migrate from Insecure Redirect URIs

In you app settings, you can see all the redirect URIs that are currently setup. Make sure to check all of them and update any non-loopback addresses that are using `http://` to `https://` if possible. If not possible remove them and add the new secure redirect URIs.

If there are any redirect URIs that are pointing to localhost, you need to update those to point to a loopback address. For example, if you have `http://localhost:8888/callback` you should update it to `http://127.0.0.1:8888/callback`. We do support dynamic ports for loopback interfaces, you can read more here .

If you see any redirect URIs that are not in use, make sure to remove them as well.

## [Reminder: OAuth Migration - 27 November 2025 | Spotify for Developers](https://developer.spotify.com/blog/2025-10-14-reminder-oauth-migration-27-nov-2025)
Published: 2025-11-27T00:00:00.000Z

Posted October 14, 2025

Spotify

TL;DR: As communicated in February 2025, Spotify will end support for the implicit grant flow, HTTP redirect URIs, and localhost aliases in their OAuth system. Existing apps must migrate to secure alternatives like Authorization Code Flow with PKCE and HTTPS redirect URIs to avoid service disruption.

On 27 November 2025, Spotify will remove support for the implicit grant flow, as well as HTTP redirect URIs and localhost aliases in our OAuth offering.

## What’s changing

- The implicit grant flow will no longer be supported.
- HTTP redirect URIs will no longer be allowed.
- Localhost aliases (such as `localhost` or similar patterns) will be prohibited.

These changes align with industry best practices and are critical to protecting both Spotify users and partners.

## Who is affected

- Existing applications that still rely on implicit grant, HTTP redirect URIs, or localhost aliases must migrate before 27 November 2025.
- New applications are already subject to these rules.

## What happens if you don’t migrate

If your app has not been updated by 27 November, it will stop working. Requests relying on deprecated flows or redirect URIs will fail.

## How to migrate

We've published detailed migration guides here and here. These cover supported OAuth flows and provides step-by-step instructions for updating redirect URIs.

## ✅ Quick migration checklist

- Stop using implicit grant flow. Switch to Authorization Code Flow with PKCE or another supported flow.
- Replace all HTTP redirect URIs with HTTPS equivalents.
- Remove any localhost aliases (e.g. `localhost`) from your redirect URIs. You can still use local IP addresses like `http://127.0.0.1`.
- Test your app thoroughly to confirm the new configuration works as expected.

## FAQ

### Why is http:// no longer supported for production apps?

Allowing `http://` redirect URIs in production apps poses security risks such as token interception. All production apps must use HTTPS redirect URIs.

### What if I don’t update my redirect URIs in time?

Any requests using `http://` or localhost aliases will fail after 27 November 2025, causing your app to stop working.

### Do I need to change anything if my app already uses HTTPS and authorization code flow?

No. If you’re already using HTTPS redirect URIs and a supported flow (e.g. Authorization Code or PKCE), you’re compliant and no further action is required.

## [Authorization Code with PKCE Flow | Spotify for Developers](https://developer.spotify.com/documentation/web-api/tutorials/code-pkce-flow)

# Authorization Code with PKCE Flow 

The authorization code flow with PKCE is the recommended authorization flow if you’re implementing authorization in a mobile app, single page web apps, or any other type of application where the client secret can’t be safely stored.

The implementation of the PKCE extension consists of the following steps:

- Code Challenge generation from a Code Verifier.
- Request authorization from the user and retrieve the authorization code.
- Request an access token from the authorization code.
- Finally, use the access token to make API calls.

...

The PKCE authorization flow starts with the creation of a code verifier. According to the PKCE standard, a code verifier is a high-entropy cryptographic random string with a length between 43 and 128 characters (the longer the better). It can contain letters, digits, underscores, periods, hyphens, or tildes.

...

Once the code verifier has been generated, we must transform (hash) it using the SHA256 algorithm. This is the value that will be sent within the user authorization request.

Let's use window.crypto.subtle.digest to generate the value using the SHA256 algorithm from the given data:

...

Let's put

...

const hashed = await sha256(codeVerifier) 

const codeChallenge = base64encode(hashed); 

## Request User Authorization

To request authorization from the user, a `GET` request must be made to the `/authorize` endpoint. This request should include the same parameters as the authorization code flow, along with two additional parameters: `code_challenge` and `code_challenge_method`:

| Query Parameter | Relevance | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| client_id | Required | The Client ID generated after registering your application. |
| response_type | Required | Set to `code`. |
| redirect_uri | Required | The URI to redirect to after the user grants or denies permission. This URI needs to have been entered in the Redirect URI allowlist that you specified when you registered your application (See the app guide). The value of `redirect_uri` here must exactly match one of the values you entered when you registered your application, including upper or lowercase, terminating slashes, and such. |
| state | Optional, but strongly recommended | This provides protection against attacks such as cross-site request forgery. See RFC-6749. |
| scope | Optional | A space-separated list of scopes. If no scopes are specified, authorization will be granted only to access publicly available information: that is, only information normally visible in the Spotify desktop, web, and mobile players. |
| code_challenge_method | Required | Set to `S256`. |
| code_challenge | Required | Set to the code challenge that your app calculated in the previous step. |

The code for requesting user authorization looks as follows:

const clientId = 'YOUR_CLIENT_ID'; 

const redirectUri = 'http://127.0.0.1:8080'; 

const scope = 'user-read-private user-read-email'; 

const authUrl = new URL("https://accounts.spotify.com/authorize") 

// generated in the previous step 

window.localStorage. setItem('code_verifier', codeVerifier); 

const params = { 

 response_type: 'code', 

 client_id: clientId, 

 scope, 

 code_challenge_method: 'S256', 

 code_challenge: codeChallenge, 

 redirect_uri: redirectUri, 

17

authUrl.search = new URLSearchParams(params). toString(); 

window.location.href = authUrl. toString(); 

The app generates a PKCE code challenge and redirects to the Spotify authorization server login page by updating the `window.location` object value. This allows the user to grant permissions to our application

Please note that the code verifier value is stored locally using the `localStorage` JavaScript property for use in the next step of the authorization flow.

### Response

If the user accepts the requested permissions, the OAuth service redirects the user back to the URL specified in the `redirect_uri` field. This callback contains two query parameters within the URL:

| Query Parameter | Value |
| --- | --- |
| code | An authorization code that can be exchanged for an access token. |
| state | The value of the `state` parameter supplied in the request. |

We must then parse the URL to retrieve the `code` parameter:

const urlParams = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search); 

let code = urlParams. get('code'); 

The `code` will be necessary to request the access token in the next step.

If the user does not accept your request or if an error has occurred, the response query string contains the following parameters:

| Query Parameter | Value |
| --- | --- |
| error | The reason authorization failed, for example: "access_denied" |
| state | The value of the `state` parameter supplied in the request. |

## Request an access token

After the user accepts the authorization request of the previous step, we can exchange the authorization code for an access token. We must send a `POST` request to the `/api/token` endpoint with the following parameters:

| Body Parameters | Relevance | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| grant_type | Required | This field must contain the value `authorization_code`. |
| code | Required | The authorization code returned from the previous request. |
| redirect_uri | Required | This parameter is used for validation only (there is no actual redirection). The value of this parameter must exactly match the value of `redirect_uri` supplied when requesting the authorization code. |
| client_id | Required | The client ID for your app, available from the developer dashboard. |
| code_verifier | Required | The value of this parameter must match the value of the `code_verifier` that your app generated in the previous step. |

The request must include the following HTTP header:

| Header Parameter | Relevance | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Content-Type | Required | Set to `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`. |

## [Increasing the security requirements for integrating with Spotify | Spotify for Developers](https://developer.spotify.com/blog/2025-02-12-increasing-the-security-requirements-for-integrating-with-spotify)
Published: 2025-02-12T00:00:00.000Z

## TL;DR

To improve security for our users, Spotify is planning to remove support for two ways of integrating with Spotify that have been replaced with more secure alternatives. This includes deprecating use of the implicit grant as well as removing support for unencrypted HTTP redirect URIs for your client.

All clients created from the 9th of April 2025 will have the new rules enforced automatically. Migration of existing clients to an acceptable state must be made by November 2025.

Here is a detailed guide with migration instructions.

## Why is this happening?

PKCE for the authorization code grant introduced clients that can’t maintain a client secret (such as mobile apps or client side web applications) to a more secure way to integrate with Spotify. Current OAuth security best practices recommend against the use of the implicit grant, and it will shortly be removed.

Similarly, the widespread adoption of HTTPS across the internet has made it much easier to accept redirects over HTTPS instead of unencrypted HTTP. By moving traffic from HTTP to HTTPS, users of applications that integrate with Spotify will be better protected against attacks that intercept network traffic.

## What next?

### The implicit grant

If you are using the implicit grant (sending `response_type=token` in your call to the authorization endpoint, or in the Android SDK using `AuthorizationResponse.Type.TOKEN`), then you will need to migrate to the authorization code grant.

If you are using a public client (one which cannot securely store a secret), you will be expected to use the PKCE extension. Confidential clients (ones which can store a secret) must use it.

### HTTP redirect URIs

Any redirect URI using HTTP will stop being supported, except loopback IP address literals such as `http://127.0.0.1` for IPv4 and `http://[::1]` for IPv6. Any invalid redirect URIs will need to be changed. You can check them under your client’s ‘settings’ tab in the developer console.

Redirects using a custom scheme will still be supported, but we recommend developers to use HTTPS redirects where possible. For mobile applications, we recommend using Android App Links and iOS Universal Links where possible.

For example:

- `http://www.example.com` could be migrated to `https://www.example.com`
- `http://localhost:3000` could be migrated to `http://127.0.0.1:3000`
- `com.example://callback` can still be used as before

Please make these checks for yourself. Comprehensive guidance will also be published via updates to the developer portal documentation.

Since we are deprecating the Implicit Grant Flow, you should migrate your application to use the Authorization Code with PKCE flow. This guide will help you migrate complete the migration for a Web Application.

## Background

[](#background)

`The Echo Nest`, before their acquisition by Spotify, represented the comprehensive algorithmic analysis of music. Each song within Spotify's [track analysis API](https://developer.spotify.com/documentation/web-api/reference/tracks/get-audio-analysis/) has been meticulously pre-analyzed: broken up into individual beats, segments, tatums, bars, and sections. With some clever elbow grease, it's possible to leverage these values with enough granularity to create meaningful visual experiences.

Since then, moving beyond the Echo Nest: I've developed a suite of tooling for *realtime* audio analysis, right in the browser: on **any** device.

Very important finding from the GitHub issue #105: "the 'audio' element lives within an iframe that is on an external cross-origin URL" — the Web Playback SDK creates its audio element inside a cross-origin iframe (`https://sdk.scdn.co/embedded/index.html`). That means we CANNOT access the audio element from the parent document (cross-origin iframe access is blocked). So `createMediaElementSource` on the Spotify stream is NOT possible. Kaleidosync v10 supports "realtime audio analysis... on any device" for multiple sources — but for Spotify it likely uses the (now-deprecated) audio-analysis API polling, not real-time DSP.

So real-time DSP on the Spotify stream is effectively blocked by the SDK's sandboxed cross-origin iframe. This kills the center-channel ducking approach on Spotify audio... unless:

Option 1: Spotify desktop/web app + system audio? No, too hacky.

Option 2: Use the "legacy polling" + Web API player control to orchestrate playback — i.e., we control playback via the Web API (play/pause/seek/volume via `PUT /v1/me/player/volume` or the SDK's player.setVolume!). # Web Playback SDK Reference

Important policy notes

- Streaming applications may not be commercial

- Keep audio content in its original form

- Do not synchronize Spotify content

- Spotify content may not be broadcasted

## Spotify.Player

### `Spotify.Player`

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| **Description** | The main constructor for initializing the Web Playback SDK. It should contain an object with the player name, volume and access token. |
| **Response** | `void` |

**Code Example:**

  

  
`_10 window.onSpotifyWebPlaybackSDKReady = () => {_10   const token = '[My Spotify Web API access token]';_10   const player = new Spotify.Player({_10     name: 'Web Playback SDK Quick Start Player',_10     getOAuthToken: cb => { cb(token); }_10   });_10 }`

| Parameter Name | Type | Description | Required |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | String | The name of the Spotify Connect player. It will be visible in other Spotify apps | **Required** |
| `getOAuthToken` | Function | This will be called every time you run Spotify.Player#connect or when a user's access token has expired (maximum of 60 minutes). You will be provided with a `callback` parameter. You will need to execute this with a valid `access_token` string for a Spotify Premium user. | **Required** |
| `volume` | Float | The default volume of the player. Represented as a decimal between **0** and **1**. Default value is **1**. | *Optional* |
| `enableMediaSession` | Boolean | If set to true, the [Media Session API](https://www.w3.org/TR/mediasession/) will be set with metadata and action handlers. Default value is **false**. | *Optional* |

### `Spotify.Player#connect`

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| **Description** | Connect our Web Playback SDK instance to Spotify with the credentials provided during initialization. |

# LRCLIB

> LRCLIB is a free, open lyrics database. Its public HTTP API returns plain lyrics, LRC-synced lyrics and Lyricsfile YAML for tracks, and accepts lyrics contributions.

Key facts:

- Base URL: https://lrclib.net
- No API key is required; anonymous access is allowed.
- Identify your client with a `User-Agent` header. `X-User-Agent` and `Lrclib-Client` are accepted where `User-Agent` cannot be changed.
- Rate limits apply per client. Honor `Retry-After` on `429` and `503` responses.
- `/api/v2/search` is a beta summary endpoint: it returns track metadata and lyrics availability flags without lyrics text. Fetch `/api/get/{id}` for the selected record.
- Responses are JSON unless noted otherwise. Check the HTTP status and `Content-Type` before parsing the body.

## Documentation

- [API reference (plain text)](https://lrclib.net/docs.txt): Complete reference for endpoints, parameters, response fields and errors. Best starting point for agents and simple HTTP clients.
- [API reference (Markdown)](https://lrclib.net/docs.md): Same content with a `.md` extension. Some static hosts serve it as `application/octet-stream`; prefer the plain-text link when a client only accepts `text/*`.
- [Full documentation in one file](https://lrclib.net/llms-full.txt): The complete API reference in a single plain-text file.
- [API reference (HTML)](https://lrclib.net/docs): Rendered version of the same documentation. Requires JavaScript.
- [Lyrics record fields](https://lrclib.net/docs#lyrics-record-fields): Shared JSON shape returned by the lyrics endpoints.
- [Errors](https://lrclib.net/docs#errors): Error names, status codes and response bodies.
- [Lyricsfile format](https://lrclib.net/lyricsfile): YAML-based lyrics format with word-level timings.
- [Database dumps](https://lrclib.net/db-dumps): Downloadable public database dumps.

## Endpoints

- [`GET /api/get`](https://lrclib.net/docs#get-lyrics-with-a-tracks-signature): Get lyrics with a track's signature.
- [`GET /api/get/{id}`](https://lrclib.net/docs#get-lyrics-by-lrclibs-id): Get lyrics by LRCLIB's ID.
- [`GET /api/search`](https://lrclib.net/docs#search-for-lyrics-records): Search for lyrics records.
- [`POST /api/publish`](https://lrclib.net/docs#publish-a-new-lyrics): Publish a new lyrics.
- [`POST /api/flag`](https://lrclib.net/docs#flag-a-lyrics): Flag a lyrics.
- [`POST /api/request-challenge`](https://lrclib.net/docs#request-a-challenge): Request a challenge.
- [`GET /api/v2/search`](https://lrclib.net/docs#search-for-lyrics-records-v2-beta): Search for lyrics records (v2 beta).

# API Documentation

> **For LLM agents:** this reference is also available as [plain text](https://lrclib.net/docs.txt); a compact index is at [llms.txt](https://lrclib.net/llms.txt).

Welcome to the documentation and specification of the LRCLIB API!

This API has generous rate limiting in place and is openly accessible to all users and applications.
No API key is required, and anonymous API access remains available.

**New update:**

- Stricter rate limits now apply to unregistered clients. See [Rate Limiting](https://lrclib.net/docs#implementation-requirements-rate-limiting).
- Developers may optionally [register applications](https://lrclib.net/docs#implementation-requirements-client-identification) to receive **higher rate limits** and an API authorization document (useful when submitting to app review).
- A beta [`GET /api/v2/search`](https://lrclib.net/docs#api-v2-beta) endpoint is available for lightweight track search without lyrics payloads. See [API v2 (beta)](https://lrclib.net/docs#api-v2-beta).

## Base URL

All endpoints are served from a single host:

```text
https://lrclib.net
```

For example, `/api/search` is reachable at `https://lrclib.net/api/search`.

The API is CORS-enabled (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`), so it can be called
directly from browser JavaScript without a proxy.

## Quickstart

Fetch your first lyrics with a single command:

```bash
curl -s 'https://lrclib.net/api/search?q=still+alive' \
  -H 'User-Agent: MyApp v1.0 (https://example.com)'
```

This returns a JSON array of matching records, each shaped like the object
described in [Lyrics record fields](https://lrclib.net/docs#lyrics-record-fields).

## Implementation Requirements

Please implement your client responsibly to avoid overloading the server. LRCLIB is a free service,
so it relies on clients behaving considerately.

### Client identification

We require you to identify your client in requests. Set the `User-Agent` header with
your application's name, version, and a link to its homepage or project page, or an
email address:

```text
LRCGET v0.2.0 (https://github.com/tranxuanthang/lrcget)
```

If modifying `User-Agent` is not possible (for example, browser JavaScript restricts
this header), you can use `X-User-Agent` or `Lrclib-Client` as alternatives.

Registration is optional: create an application in the [developer portal](https://lrclib.net/developers)
to receive **higher rate limits**, a shareable API authorization document (useful when
submitting to app review), and a way for us to contact you if your integration
misbehaves. There are two access models:

- **Client-side applications** identify themselves with the public `Lrclib-App-Id`
  header. The ID is not a secret, so it is safe to ship in a client.
- **Server-side applications** authenticate with a secret `Lrclib-Api-Key` header.
  Keep the key on your server — never embed it in a client application. Keys can be
  rotated from the portal by creating a new one and revoking the old one.

Both headers are optional, but invalid values are rejected with `401 Unauthorized`
(see [Errors](https://lrclib.net/docs#errors)). See [Rate Limiting](https://lrclib.net/docs#implementation-requirements-rate-limiting)
for the allowance each model receives.

### Rate Limiting

Requests are limited per client. The exact limits are not part of the API contract:
the figures below are approximations of the current settings and may change at any
time without notice.

| How the request identifies itself | Approximate allowance |
| --------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| Generic client (no `User-Agent`, browser, `curl`, or a common HTTP library) | ~45 requests/min per IP |
| Identified client (`User-Agent` naming your application) | ~90 requests/min per IP |
| Registered client-side application (`Lrclib-App-Id`) | ~180 requests/min per IP, plus an app-wide allowance (~6,000 requests/min) |
| Registered server-side application (`Lrclib-Api-Key`) | app-wide allowance only (~6,000 requests/min) |

Allowances are per IP address (IPv6 addresses count as `/64` blocks) and refill
steadily with a small burst buffer. Anonymous access remains enough for normal
use; registered applications receive higher allowances (see
[Client identification](https://lrclib.net/docs#implementation-requirements-client-identification)).

When a limit is exceeded, the server responds with `429 Too Many Requests`, a
`Retry-After` header specifying how many seconds to wait, and a JSON body naming
the limiting scope (`ip` or `application`):

```json
{
  "message": "Too many requests from this IP address. …",
  "name": "RateLimitExceeded",
  "statusCode": 429,
  "scope": "ip"
}
```

Your client **must** honor `Retry-After`. Wait at least the given number of
seconds before retrying, and add a small random jitter (for example, up to 30% of
the delay) so that many clients throttled at the same moment do not retry in a
synchronized wave. Ignoring `Retry-After` and continuing to send requests may
result in a temporary ban.

Under extreme floods the network edge may reject requests before they reach the
API; those responses are not guaranteed to be JSON. Always rely on the status code
and the `Retry-After` header rather than parsing the body.

### Request Throttling

To avoid hitting rate limits, send requests sequentially by waiting for each one to finish
before starting the next. Additionally, add a short delay between requests (200–500 ms),
especially for batch operations like scanning a full music library.

## Lyrics record fields

The v1 lyrics endpoints (`/api/get`, `/api/get/{id}` and `/api/search`) use
the same JSON object shape:

| Field | Type | Description |
| ----- | ---- | ----------- |
| id | number | Unique, stable ID of the lyrics record |
| name | string | Alias of `trackName`, kept for backwards compatibility |
| trackName | string | Title of the track |
| artistName | string | Name of the artist |
| albumName | string | Name of the album |
| duration | number | Track duration in seconds |
| instrumental | boolean | `true` when the track has no lyrics |
| hasWordSync | boolean | `true` when `lyricsfile` contains word-level timings (`lines[].words`) |
| plainLyrics | string \| null | Plain, unsynced lyrics. `null` for instrumental records |
| syncedLyrics | string \| null | LRC-formatted lyrics with line timestamps. `null` for instrumental records |
| lyricsfile | string | Raw Lyricsfile YAML document. Every record is guaranteed to include one |

> The beta `/api/v2/search` endpoint returns a smaller summary object without
> lyrics text. See [v2 search summary fields](https://lrclib.net/docs#v2-search-summary-fields).

## Errors

Failed requests return a JSON object with the HTTP status code repeated in the
`statusCode` field:

```json
{
  "message": "duration: must be between 1 and 3600",
  "name": "ValidationError",
  "statusCode": 400
}
```

| Status | `name` | Meaning |
| ------ | ------ | ------- |
| 400 | `ValidationError` | A parameter failed validation, for example an empty `track_name` or a `duration` outside the allowed range |
| 400 | `IncorrectPublishTokenError` | The `X-Publish-Token` header is missing, malformed, already used, or expired |
| 401 | `InvalidAppIdError` | The `Lrclib-App-Id` header is not a registered application |
| 401 | `MissingApiKeyError` | The `Lrclib-App-Id` belongs to a server-side application, but no `Lrclib-Api-Key` was sent |
| 401 | `InvalidApiKeyError` | The `Lrclib-Api-Key` is unknown or revoked, or does not belong to the application in `Lrclib-App-Id` |
| 404 | `TrackNotFound` | No lyrics record matched the request |
| 429 | `RateLimitExceeded` | Rate limit exceeded; see [Rate Limiting](https://lrclib.net/docs#implementation-requirements-rate-limiting). Honor the `Retry-After` header. Rejections at the network edge may not be JSON |
| 500 | `UnknownError` | Unexpected server error, try again later |
| 503 | `ServerOverloaded` | The server is temporarily busy; retry after the `Retry-After` header (usually 1 second) |

**Note:** Requests with malformed or missing query parameters are rejected by the
framework before they reach the API logic and return a plain-text response instead:

```text
Failed to deserialize query string: missing field `artist_name`
```

Always check the status code and `Content-Type` before assuming the body is JSON.

## Supported Endpoints

The endpoints in this section are the stable v1 API. The beta v2 search
endpoint is documented separately in [API v2 (beta)](https://lrclib.net/docs#api-v2-beta).

### Get lyrics with a track's signature

`GET /api/get`

Attempt to find the best match of lyrics for the track. You must provide
the track title and the artist name. Providing the album name and the
track's duration in seconds is recommended and improves the matching
precision.

If no match is found, the API returns `404 Not Found`. Missing tracks can
be picked up by the background lyrics fetching service and may become
available in a later request.

**Note:** The provided `duration` is crucial. LRCLIB will attempt to provide the lyrics
only when the duration matches the record in LRCLIB's database, or at least with
a difference of ±2 seconds in duration.

### Publish a new lyrics

`POST /api/publish`

**Note:** This API is experimental and subject to potential changes in the future.

Publish a new lyrics to LRCLIB database. This API can be called anonymously, and no registration is required.

If `plainLyrics`, `syncedLyrics` and `lyricsfile` are all left empty, the track will be marked as instrumental.

If a `lyricsfile` is provided, it is stored as-is and takes precedence:
any `plainLyrics` and `syncedLyrics` in the same request are ignored.
A Lyricsfile that contains word-level timings (`lines[].words`) marks the
record as word-synced (`hasWordSync: true` in subsequent API responses);
records published with only `plainLyrics` or `syncedLyrics` are never
word-synced.

All previous revisions of the lyrics will still be kept when publishing lyrics for a track that already has existing lyrics.

#### Obtaining the Publish Token

Every `POST /api/publish` request must include a fresh,
valid Publish Token in the `X-Publish-Token` header. Each Publish Token can only be used once.

The Publish Token consists of two parts: a `prefix` and a `nonce` concatenated with a colon (`{prefix}:{nonce}`).

To obtain a `prefix`, you need to make a request to the `POST /api/request-challenge` API.
This will provide you with a fresh prefix string and a target string.

To find a valid `nonce`, you must solve a proof-of-work cryptographic challenge
using the provided `prefix` and `target`.
For implementation examples, please refer to
[the source code of LRCGET](https://github.com/tranxuanthang/lrcget/blob/main/src-tauri/src/lrclib/challenge_solver.rs).

#### Request header

| Header name      | Required | Description                                                         |
| ---------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| X-Publish-Token  | true     | A Publish Token that can be retrieved via solving a cryptographic challenge |

#### Request JSON body parameters

| Field        | Required | Type   | Description                     |
| ------------ | -------- | ------ | ------------------------------- |
| trackName    | true     | string | Title of the track              |
| artistName   | true     | string | Track's artist name             |
| albumName    | true     | string | Track's album name              |
| duration     | true     | number | Track's duration                |
| plainLyrics  | false    | string | Plain lyrics for the track      |
| syncedLyrics | false    | string | Synchronized lyrics for the track |
| lyricsfile   | false    | string | Raw Lyricsfile YAML for the track. When provided, `plainLyrics` and `syncedLyrics` are ignored |

#### Response

Success response: 201 Created

Failed response (incorrect Publish Token):

```json
{
  "message": "The provided publish token is incorrect",
  "name": "IncorrectPublishTokenError",
  "statusCode": 400
}
```


### Flag a lyrics

`POST /api/flag`

Report the currently published lyrics of a track (for example, wrong lyrics,
wrong track metadata, or a copyright violation). The flag is recorded against
the track's current lyrics.

Every `POST /api/flag` request must include a fresh, valid Publish Token in the
`X-Publish-Token` header, obtained the same way as described in the
"Publish a new lyrics" section.

#### Request header

| Header name      | Required | Description                                                         |
| ---------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| X-Publish-Token  | true     | A Publish Token that can be retrieved via solving a cryptographic challenge |

#### Request JSON body parameters

| Field    | Required | Type   | Description                         |
| -------- | -------- | ------ | ----------------------------------- |
| trackId  | true     | number | ID of the track to flag             |
| content  | false    | string | Optional reason for the flag        |

#### Example request

```http
POST /api/flag
X-Publish-Token: VXMwW2qPfW2gkCNSl1i708NJkDghtAyU:0000a1b2c3d4e5f6

{
  "trackId": 3396226,
  "content": "The lyrics don't match the audio"
}
```

#### Response

Success response: 201 Created

Failed response (incorrect Publish Token):

```json
{
  "message": "The provided publish token is incorrect",
  "name": "IncorrectPublishTokenError",
  "statusCode": 400
}
```


### Request a challenge

`POST /api/request-challenge`

**Note:** This API is experimental and subject to potential changes in the future.

Generate a pair of `prefix` and `target` strings for the cryptographic challenge.
Each challenge has an expiration time of 5 minutes.

The challenge's solution is a `nonce`, which can be used to create a Publish Token for submitting lyrics to LRCLIB.

#### Example response

```json
{
  "prefix": "VXMwW2qPfW2gkCNSl1i708NJkDghtAyU",
  "target": "000000FF00000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000"
}
```


## API v2 (beta)

Beta

The v2 API is being introduced with a lightweight search endpoint. It is
intended for clients that need to find tracks first and fetch lyrics only for
the selected result. The v1 endpoints remain available and unchanged.

> **Beta notice:** the v2 search endpoint and its response shape may change

### v2 search summary fields

The v2 search endpoint returns track metadata and lyrics availability flags,
but does not include any lyrics text or Lyricsfile YAML.

| Field | Type | Description |
| ----- | ---- | ----------- |
| id | number | Unique, stable ID of the track |
| trackName | string | Title of the track |
| artistName | string | Name of the artist |
| albumName | string | Name of the album |
| duration | number | Track duration in seconds |
| instrumental | boolean | `true` when the track has no lyrics |
| hasWordSync | boolean | `true` when the current lyrics contain word-level timings |
| hasPlainLyrics | boolean | `true` when plain lyrics are available |
| hasSyncedLyrics | boolean | `true` when LRC-synced lyrics are available |
| hasLyricsfile | boolean | `true` when a raw Lyricsfile YAML document is available |

with the returned `id`. The v1 lyrics record shape is described in
[Lyrics record fields](https://lrclib.net/docs#lyrics-record-fields).

### Search for lyrics records (v2 beta)

`GET /api/v2/search`

Search for tracks and return lightweight metadata without lyrics payloads.
This endpoint is intended for clients that search first and then request the
selected track's lyrics from `/api/get/{id}`.

At least ONE of the two parameters, `q` OR `track_name`, must be present.
If neither is provided, an empty array is returned.

The response contains up to 20 results and does not support pagination.

[v2 search summary fields](https://lrclib.net/docs#v2-search-summary-fields); unlike v1 search,

Feasible: Yes, with one important design adaptation — Spotify's Web Playback SDK streams audio inside a cross-origin DRM iframe that cannot be tapped into the Web Audio API (confirmed via SDK docs/issues). export function cleanTitle(name) {
  let t = name;
  // strip bracketed groups: (..), [..], {..} repeatedly
  const bracket = /\s*[([{][^)\]}]*[)\]}]/g;
  let prev; do { prev = t; t = t.replace(bracket, ' '); } while (t !== prev);
  // strip dash suffixes containing keywords
  const dashParts = t.split(/\s[-–—]\s+/);
  if (dashParts.length > 1) {
    const kw = /(remaster|remastered|version|edit|mix|deluxe|anniversary|bonus|mono|stereo|feat|ft|featuring|single|radio|live|session|acoustic)/i;
    t = dashParts.filter(p => !kw.test(p)).join(' - ') || dashParts[0];
  }
  return t.replace(/\s+/g,' ').trim() || name.trim();
}
export function cleanArtists(names: string[]) {
  const primary = names[0] ?? '';
  // if primary contains 'feat'/'with'/'&'/'x' take before

  return m.trim() || primary.trim();
}
